values: The sum of all anabolic and catabolic chemical reactions that take place in the body.
The process whereby smaller, simpler molecules are combined into larger, more complex substances.
The process by which larger, more complex substances are broken down into smaller, simpler molecules.
Encompasses both energy-consuming and energy-releasing processes.
Requires an investment of energy to form new chemical bonds.
Releases energy as chemical bonds are broken down.
The ability of an organism or system to adjust to changes in its internal and external environments.
The physical motion of individual organs, cells, or actions at the joints of the body.
Detects stimuli (like increased body temperature or a threat) and triggers a corresponding reaction.
Executes the physical action required for life, such as muscles contracting, blood circulating, or physically moving away from danger.
All of the changes the body goes through in life.
The process in which unspecialized cells become specialized in structure and function.
The process of increasing in physical size.
The formation of a new organism from parent organisms.
The overarching category that inherently includes differentiation, growth, and tissue repair.
A specific mechanism within development that dictates cell tasks.
Achieved by increasing the number of cells, non-cellular material, or cell size.
Unlike the other three, which happen within an individual, reproduction aims to ensure the continuation of the species by creating a new individual.
A gas that makes up about 20 percent of atmospheric air.
A chemical substance obtained from foods and beverages critical to survival.
The most critical nutrient and largest component of cells, blood, and interstitial fluid.
Energy-yielding macronutrients.
A macronutrient that primarily supplies amino acids.
A key reactant in the chemical reactions that keep the body alive, specifically ATP production.
Provides the fundamental building blocks and energy for the body.
Dissolves and transports functional chemicals, regulates temperature, and lubricates joints.
Broken down by the digestive system and used in metabolic processes that convert them to ATP for energy.
Serves as the building blocks of the body itself.
The measure of internal body heat, normally kept within a narrow range around 37°C (98.6°F).
The force exerted by a substance in contact with another substance.
Maintains the precise environment required for proteins (enzymes) to facilitate chemical reactions; extreme deviations halt metabolism.
Atmospheric pressure keeps blood gases dissolved and enables the ability to breathe, while blood pressure ensures blood reaches all body tissues.
The ideal, specific physiological value around which a parameter fluctuates.
The restricted set of values that is optimally healthful and stable.
e.g., The exact target body temperature is approximately 37°C (98.6°F).
e.g., Body temperature is allowed to safely fluctuate a few degrees above or below the set point.
A change that drives a physiological parameter beyond its normal range.
A component that monitors a physiological value.
A component that compares the reported value to the normal range.
A component that causes a change to reverse the situation.
Initiates the feedback loop.
Reports the value to the control center.
Activates the effector if the value deviates too much from the set point.
Returns the physiological value back to the normal range.
A homeostatic mechanism that reverses a deviation from the set point.
A mechanism that intensifies a change in the body's physiological condition.
Works continuously to maintain body parameters within their normal range (e.g., regulating blood glucose or temperature).
Moves the system farther away from the normal range until a definite end point is reached (e.g., childbirth or blood clotting).
A measure of the amount of matter in an object.
Any physical substance that occupies space and has mass.
A pure substance that cannot be created or broken down by ordinary chemical means.
A property possessed by all matter.
The physical "stuff" of the universe, composed entirely of elements.
The 92 fundamental building blocks that combine to form all matter.
Matter that maintains its shape and density.
Matter that flows freely but maintains a constant volume.
Compressible matter that expands to fill its container.
Bones, teeth, and mineral crystals.
Blood plasma, water, interstitial fluid, and cytosol.
Oxygen, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen dissolved in fluids or in the respiratory tract.
Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen.
Elements like calcium, phosphorus, potassium, and sodium.
Elements like boron, cobalt, copper, and zinc.
Make up the vast majority (over 95%) of the human body.
Make up a small fraction of the body, but are essential for nerve, muscle, and bone function.
Each account for less than 1.0% of the body's composition, but are still required for physiological processes.
The smallest unit of an element.
The center of the atom.
A subatomic particle.
A subatomic particle.
A subatomic particle.
An area of space a given distance from the nucleus.
Electrically neutral if protons equal electrons.
Contains nearly all of the atom's mass.
Heavy, with a positive electrical charge.
Heavy, with no electrical charge.
Nearly no mass, with a negative electrical charge.
Contains the grouping of electrons.
A one- or two-letter abbreviation used to identify an element (e.g., "O" for oxygen).
The exact number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The sum of the number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
Acts as a shorthand placeholder in chemical equations and text.
Uniquely identifies the element.
Determines the overall mass of the atom and identifies isotopes.
An unstable, heavy variation of an element that differs in its number of neutrons.
An atom with an overall positive or negative charge.
An atom possessing the same number of positively charged protons and negatively charged electrons.
Gives off subatomic particles or electromagnetic energy as it decays.
Formed when an atom donates or accepts one or more electrons to fill its valence shell.
Is electrically balanced and neutral.
Two or more atoms covalently bonded together.
A substance composed of two or more different elements joined by chemical bonds.
A molecule can consist of atoms of the same element (e.g., H₂ or O₂) or different elements.
All compounds are molecules, but not all molecules are compounds, because compounds must contain different elements (e.g., glucose).
An atom with a negative charge.
An atom with a positive charge.
Created when an atom accepts an electron to fill its valence shell.
Created when an atom donates an electron to empty its valence shell.
The electrical attraction between an anion and a cation.
A chemical bond in which two atoms share electrons equally, rendering the molecule electrically balanced.
A covalent bond in which electrons are shared unequally, creating regions of opposite charge within the molecule.
A weak dipole-dipole bond between a covalently bonded hydrogen atom and a second electronegative atom.
Dissociates into separate ions (electrolytes).
Does not readily dissolve in water (hydrophobic).
Dissolves readily in water (hydrophilic).
Links separate water molecules together to give water its unique properties.
An electrical property (positive or negative) resulting from the gain or loss of electrons in an atom.
An atom's inherent tendency to attract shared electrons towards itself within a chemical bond.
Creates fully formed anions and cations.
Creates partial negative and positive charges (dipoles) within polar covalent molecules like water.
The physical or chemical action powered by the expenditure of energy.
The energy matter possesses because of the positioning or structure of its components.
The form of energy powering any type of matter in physical motion.
The form of potential energy in which energy is stored within chemical bonds.
Driven by the conversion of potential energy into kinetic energy.
Stores energy for future use, like a brick wall holding energy after being built.
Releases energy to create movement, like the energy used to lift a brick.
Invests and releases energy during chemical reactions in the body when bonds are built or broken.
The one or more starting substances that enter into a chemical reaction.
The one or more new substances produced by a chemical reaction.
A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without undergoing any permanent change itself.
A specific type of biological catalyst composed of protein or RNA.
The raw materials that will be changed.
The final result of the rearranged reactants.
Speeds up the reaction between reactants by lowering the required activation energy.
Facilitates nearly all chemical reactions in the human body with high specificity.
An anabolic chemical reaction that joins formerly separate components together.
A catabolic chemical reaction that breaks down a larger substance into its constituent parts.
A chemical reaction in which bonds are both formed and broken.
Requires an investment of energy to form the new bonds.
Releases the potential energy that was stored in the broken bonds.
Energy is absorbed, stored, and released as components are rearranged.
The measure of thermal energy.
The number of particles present within a given space.
The total amount of physical space containing the particles.
Higher temperatures increase the kinetic energy of particles, making them move faster and react more readily.
Higher concentration means more particles are present, increasing the likelihood of collisions and reactions.
Decreasing the volume increases the pressure and concentration of the particles, speeding up the reaction.
Chemical reactions that release more energy than they absorb.
Chemical reactions that absorb more energy than they release.
The "threshold" level of energy needed to break the bonds in the reactants to start a reaction.
Catabolism of food for fuel, which releases heat and energy.
Synthesis of new molecules, which requires an energy input often provided by exergonic reactions.
Lowered significantly by enzymes to allow endergonic and exergonic reactions to occur at body temperature.

sectionTitle: Section 2.4: Inorganic Compounds Essential to Human Functioning

values: A substance that contains both carbon and hydrogen.
A substance that does not contain both carbon and hydrogen.
Essential chemical substances obtained from foods and beverages.
Synthesized via covalent bonds within living organisms to build body structures.
Includes vital molecules like water, salts, acids, and bases.
Includes both inorganic (water, minerals) and organic (carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins) compounds critical for survival.
A homogeneous liquid mixture where a solute (substance being dissolved) is evenly distributed throughout a solvent (the liquid doing the dissolving).
A liquid mixture where solute particles are large enough to make the mixture opaque, but do not settle.
A liquid mixture in which a heavier substance is temporarily suspended but will eventually settle out.
The universal solvent in the body, making up about 70% of an adult's body weight.
Sugar or salts dissolved evenly in blood plasma.
Thyroid hormone stored as a thick protein mixture, or milk.
Red blood cells suspended in blood plasma, which will settle to the bottom if left in a tube.
Dissolves ionic and polar compounds to facilitate nearly all chemical reactions.
A reaction where a molecule of water disrupts a compound, breaking its bonds.
A reaction where two reactants bond together, giving up a hydrogen atom and a hydroxyl group to release a water molecule.
The addition of a phosphate group to an organic compound.
Consumes water to break polymers down into monomers.
Creates water as a byproduct when building polymers from monomers.
Often requires an energy investment, such as converting ADP into high-energy ATP.
Acids release hydrogen ions (H+) in solution, while bases release hydroxyl ions (OH-) or accept H+.
The negative, base-10 logarithm of the hydrogen ion (H+) concentration of a solution.
A substance that dissociates in water into ions other than H+ or OH-.
A solution of a weak acid and its conjugate base.
Acids (like HCl) aid digestion, while bases (like bicarbonate) neutralize strong acids to prevent tissue damage.
Measures relative acidity or alkalinity; normal human blood tightly regulates between 7.35 and 7.45.
Provides vital electrolytes (like Na+ and Cl-) that conduct electrical currents for nerve impulses and muscle contraction.
Prevents radical fluctuations in pH by neutralizing small amounts of excess acids or bases in body fluids.

sectionTitle: Section 2.5: Organic Compounds Essential to Human Functioning

values: Organic molecules composed of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen (hydrated carbon).
The basic single-sugar monomers of carbohydrates.
A pair of monosaccharides linked by a glycosidic bond.
Large polymers consisting of hundreds to thousands of monosaccharides.
The body's preferred and most common source of fuel for ATP production.
Glucose, fructose, and galactose (hexoses); ribose and deoxyribose (pentoses).
Sucrose (table sugar), lactose (milk sugar), and maltose.
Used for energy storage (starch, glycogen) or structural components (cellulose).
Simple carbohydrates (monosaccharides and disaccharides).
A polymer of glucose stored in animal tissues.
Polymers of glucose occurring in long or branched chains.
A structural polysaccharide that is the primary component of green plant cell walls.
Provide readily absorbed, immediate energy fuel.
The human body's way to store excess glucose, mostly in the liver and muscles.
A common, easy-to-digest plant-based food source.
Indigestible to humans, but serves as essential dietary fiber for digestive health.
A diverse group of hydrophobic, mostly hydrocarbon organic compounds.
The physical components of a fat: A 3-carbon glycerol backbone attached to long hydrocarbon fatty acid chains.
Fatty acid chains containing the maximum number of hydrogen atoms and no double carbon bonds.
Fatty acid chains containing one or more double carbon bonds.
Do not form true solutions in water, serving as excellent long-term energy storage.
Form the structure of triglycerides via dehydration synthesis.
Straight, rigid chains that pack tightly and are solid at room temperature (e.g., butter).
Kinked chains that cannot pack tightly and are liquid at room temperature (e.g., olive oil).
Dietary fats consisting of a glycerol backbone and three fatty acids.
A diglyceride attached to a charged phosphate group.
Ring-shaped lipids built on a foundation of four interlocking hydrocarbon rings.
Signaling lipids derived from unsaturated fatty acids.
The most abundant lipid in body tissues, serving as a major fuel source and thermal insulation.
Forms the cell membrane bilayer due to having a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails.
Cholesterol is a crucial cell membrane component and the building block for steroid hormones and bile salts.
Important for regulating several physiological processes, including inflammation and pain.
"Water-fearing" molecules that do not readily dissolve in water.
"Water-loving" molecules that easily dissolve in water.
Substances that dissolve easily in water-based bodily fluids.
Substances that dissolve in lipids and require dietary fat for absorption.
Nonpolar molecules like triglyceride fats and oils.
Polar covalent compounds and ionic compounds (like salt and sugar).
Most B vitamins and Vitamin C (excess is excreted in urine).
Vitamins A, D, E, and K (can accumulate in the body's lipid stores).
The nitrogen-containing monomers that make up proteins.
The two universal functional groups found on all amino acids: an alkaline amino group and an acidic carboxyl group.
A variable functional group attached to the central carbon of an amino acid.
A covalent bond formed by dehydration synthesis that links two amino acids.
Just 20 different amino acids combine to build thousands of different human proteins.
Allows every amino acid to act as an excellent buffer for acid-base balance.
Gives each of the 20 amino acids its unique chemical properties (size, polarity).
Strings together short peptides or long polypeptides to build functional proteins.
Primary: the sequence of amino acids in the chain. Secondary: local folding patterns like alpha-helices or beta-pleated sheets.
Tertiary: the overall 3D shape of a single polypeptide. Quaternary: multiple polypeptide chains assembling together.
A change in the functional structure of a molecule through physical or chemical means.
Stabilized by peptide bonds and local hydrogen bonds.
Creates the highly specific functional shapes required for enzymes and structural proteins like hemoglobin.
Extreme heat or pH can cause proteins to unfold and lose their ability to perform their jobs.
Proteins are large polymers of amino acids. Enzymes are a highly reactive globular type of protein.
Substrates are the specific reactants that fit like puzzle pieces into an enzyme's active site to be converted into a product.
A catalyst is a chemical change agent that lowers the activation energy (threshold energy) needed for a reaction to occur.
While proteins serve many structural roles (like collagen), enzymes function strictly as biological catalysts.
The specific jigsaw-like match between the substrate and active site ensures enzymes only trigger specific reactions to yield precise products.
By lowering activation energy, the enzyme (catalyst) allows vital chemical reactions to happen fast enough to sustain human life.
Nucleic acids are macromolecules built from monomer subunits called nucleotides.
Deoxyribonucleic acid, a double-stranded nucleic acid.
Ribonucleic acid, a single-stranded nucleic acid.
Adenosine triphosphate, a high-energy nucleotide containing three phosphate groups.
Carry and express genetic information, and transfer energy.
Permanently stores the genetic code containing the instructions to build the body.
Translates the DNA code to manufacture proteins.
Acts as the universal energy currency to fuel cellular work.
The nitrogen-containing component of a nucleotide (Adenine, Cytosine, Guanine, Thymine, or Uracil).
A 5-carbon sugar that acts as the backbone of a nucleotide. Deoxyribose has one less oxygen atom than Ribose.
A functional group consisting of phosphorus and oxygen.
Protrudes from the backbone to form hydrogen bonds that encode genetic information.
DNA contains deoxyribose, while RNA and ATP contain ribose.
Bonds with pentose sugars to form the "backbone" of DNA and RNA, or stores massive potential energy in ATP.
Nitrogen-containing bases with a double-ring structure.
Nitrogen-containing bases with a single-ring structure.
Adenine and Guanine are utilized in both DNA and RNA.
Cytosine is used in both. Thymine is used exclusively in DNA, while Uracil is used exclusively in RNA.
